Sampled HR@10 does not reliably estimate full-catalog HR@10: candidate sampling can reverse model comparisons even in expectation ([Krichene & Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). Recent evidence supports stratified diagnosis: a 2024 sequential-recommendation study found aggregate metrics conceal head/mid/tail differences, with random negative training favoring head items and popularity-based sampling trading overall accuracy for more balanced performance ([Prakash et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)). RecSys 2025 research examines sampling reliability through fidelity, resolution, robustness and recovery of model rankings ([On the Reliability of Sampling Strategies](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086)). These findings motivate candidate-set audits; they do not establish a BERT4Rec-specific semantic diagnostic.

Proposed audit: use fixed training-prefix/next-item pairs, omit the target from bidirectional input, append BERT4Rec’s mask, and score every candidate with the same category checkpoint. Compare equal-sized, deduplicated sets of uniform candidates, candidates matched to the target’s training-frequency band, and title/description-similar candidates selected using local lexical similarity. Exclude prefix-seen items; calculate frequencies from training data only. Report target-rank percentiles, positive–candidate score margins, top-10 hit flips and variation across repeated candidate draws; compare against full-catalog target ranks where affordable. Stratify by prefix length and target frequency, reporting counts and uncertainty per category. Treat these as proposed descriptive diagnostics: text similarity does not establish substitutability, and unobserved items are not verified dislikes. Keep every audit separate from the pinned host evaluator; retain macro validation HR@10 for model selection.
